docs.title: ClassLink
docs.text:
UCS503P — Software Engineering Project, TIET

ClassLink is a BLE-based classroom attendance system. A teacher's phone advertises a short-lived Bluetooth Low Energy token for an active session; enrolled students' phones scan for that token while physically nearby, collect proximity evidence, authenticate locally, and submit a signed attendance claim to a server-authoritative backend.

ClassLink does not claim to prove that the human owner of a phone is present. It verifies that a bound, locally authenticated device observed a valid classroom beacon under a configured proximity policy.

docs.title: Current status
docs.text:
The repository contains two working pieces and one in progress.

  • Backend (done, tested). A FastAPI service on Supabase Postgres with row level security, rotating BLE tokens, device signed attendance claims, a live roster, corrections with a mandatory reason, an audit trail, and CSV export. See backend/.
  • Offline proof of concept app (done). A Flutter app that proves the core BLE mechanism: the teacher advertises, the student scans and checks in by proximity, and results export to CSV on the device.
  • Mobile integration with the backend (in progress). Sign in, device key signing, rotating token advertising, and the live roster in the app. The SRS marks each requirement as Done, POC, or Planned.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
• code/ — the Flutter application source.
  • Software Requirements Specification — requirements, threat model, API summary, and test traceability.
  • UML diagrams — use case, class, sequence, activity, component, deployment, and state diagrams for the current POC.
  • journals/ — weekly progress journals, one per team member.
  • project-proposal/ — the project proposal (LaTeX source and PDF).
  • project-srs/ — the SRS as LaTeX and PDF, generated from the Markdown in docs/srs/.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we'll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: "Students can't find answers fast." Solution: "Add an FAQ search." Evaluation criterion: "Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5."

  • Problem: "The app is slow." Solution: "Optimize queries." Evaluation criterion: "Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production."

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and "time-to-replace"
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Deployment and Pilot Runbook
docs.text: This runbook takes ClassLink from a clean checkout to a running pilot. The steps that need an account, a payment method, or a secret belong to a person on the team. Nothing here asks you to put a secret in the repository.

docs.title: What you deploy
docs.text: Piece Where it runs How it gets there Postgres, Auth Supabase project You create the project and apply one SQL file API Any container host (Render blueprint included) render.yaml, or the image from GitHub Container Registry Android app Students' and teachers' phones The APK from the android-release workflow iOS app iPhones Built from code/ in Xcode with the same --dart-define values

docs.title: 1. Create the Supabase project
docs.text:
1. Create a project at supabase.com. Note the region and the database password.
  2. Open SQL Editor, paste backend/migrations/0001_init.sql, and run it. It creates the tables, the row level security policies, and the helper functions. It does not seed any data.
  3. Collect three values:
  4. Connection string. Project Settings, Database, then the connection string for the postgres role. This bypasses row level security, so it stays on the server only.
  5. JWT secret. Project Settings, API, then JWT Settings. The API verifies user tokens with it. The legacy shared secret is supported. Projects that sign with asymmetric keys need JWKS verification, which is not built yet.
  6. Anon key and project URL. The mobile app needs these to sign users in. They are safe to ship in the app.
  7. Under Authentication, turn on the sign in method you want for the pilot (email with password is the simplest). Consider restricting sign up to your college email domain.

docs.title: 2. Generate the token secret
docs.text:
python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))"

Store it as CLASSLINK_TOKEN_HMAC_SECRET. Changing it invalidates every token already advertised, which is harmless between sessions.

docs.title: Option A: Render
docs.text:
1. In Render, choose New, Blueprint and pick this repository. It reads render.yaml.
  2. Fill in the four secrets when prompted: CLASSLINK_DATABASE_URL, CLASSLINK_JWT_SECRET, CLASSLINK_TOKEN_HMAC_SECRET, and CLASSLINK_TEACHER_EMAILS (a JSON list such as ["name@thapar.edu"]).
  3. After the first deploy, open https://<your-service>/readyz. It must answer {"status":"ready"}. Then open /docs for the live API reference.

docs.title: Option B: any container host
docs.text: The backend-image workflow publishes ghcr.io/vrishanknehru/classlink-backend on every push to main and on tags. Run it with the same four environment variables plus CLASSLINK_ENVIRONMENT=production, behind HTTPS.

docs.title: Settings you may tune
docs.text:
All are CLASSLINK_* variables. backend/.env.example lists the required ones.

Variable Default Meaning TOKEN_PERIOD_SECONDS 15 How often the BLE token rotates (5 to 120) TOKEN_GRACE_EPOCHS 1 How many old epochs still validate CHALLENGE_TTL_SECONDS 120 How long a nonce lives CLAIM_MAX_AGE_SECONDS 60 Allowed gap between the phone's observation time and the server clock

docs.title: 4. Make the first teacher
docs.text: The teacher role comes from CLASSLINK_TEACHER_EMAILS. Add the teacher's email, redeploy, then have them sign in and create their profile. Anyone not on the list becomes a student. There is no in app way to grant teacher.

docs.title: 5. Build and distribute the APK
docs.text:
1. In Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions > Variables, add CLASSLINK_API_BASE_URL (the API's https address), SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_ANON_KEY. The workflow bakes them into the APK. To build by hand: 
    cd code
flutter build apk --release \
  --dart-define=API_BASE_URL=https://classlink-api.onrender.com \
  --dart-define=SUPABASE_URL=https://abcd.supabase.co \
  --dart-define=SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=eyJ...
    For iPhones use flutter build ipa with the same flags and your Apple team.
  2. In the GitHub repository settings, add four secrets for release signing: ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64, ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD, ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS, and ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD. Create the keystore yourself and keep a backup. Losing it means you cannot update installed apps. 
    keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore classlink.jks -alias classlink \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
base64 -w0 classlink.jks   # paste as ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64
  3. Push a tag: git tag v0.2.0 && git push origin v0.2.0. The workflow runs the analyzer and tests, builds app-release.apk, and attaches it to the release.
  4. Students install the APK by sideloading it. Without the four secrets the workflow still builds, signed with the debug key. That is fine for a pilot and not for the Play Store.

The Android application id and the iOS bundle id are com.classlink.app. Change them before any store upload if the college wants its own domain, because they cannot change afterwards.

docs.title: 6. Pilot checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] /readyz is green and /docs loads.
  • [ ] A teacher account exists and can create a classroom.
  • [ ] Two student phones of different models joined the classroom.
  • [ ] Each student phone bound its device key.
  • [ ] One test session ran end to end and the CSV export opened correctly.
  • [ ] Participants know what the app stores (name, roll number, email, device key, attendance) and that it never collects location.

docs.title: 7. Operating it
docs.text:
• Health. Point an uptime monitor at /readyz.
  • Backups. Turn on Supabase backups for the project. Attendance records are the product.
  • What happened to a claim. Rejections and acceptances live in audit_events. Example: 
    select created_at, details->>'reason' as reason, details->>'stage' as stage
from audit_events where action = 'claim_rejected' order by id desc limit 50;
  • Rotating secrets. Change the token secret or JWT secret in the host's dashboard and redeploy. Changing the JWT secret signs everyone out.
  • Rollback. Redeploy the previous image tag. Migrations are additive in version 1.0, so no database rollback is needed.

docs.title: Local development
docs.text:
docker compose up --build        # Postgres + API on :8000
python backend/scripts/dev_token.py teacher@example.edu

The script prints a user id and a bearer token. Insert the user into auth.users first (the script's docstring shows the command). The compose stack uses throwaway credentials and is not a deployment target.

docs.title: Evaluation Data
docs.text:
This folder holds the raw measurements for the evaluation in the SRS (Appendix D). Rules:

  1. Real runs only. Every row comes from an executed test on real phones in a real room. Never pre-fill or estimate.
  2. Raw before summary. Commit the raw CSV first. Compute tables and figures from it afterwards, and name the CSV a figure came from.
  3. One file per session of testing. Name files YYYY-MM-DD-room-label.csv.

Start from TEMPLATE.csv, which has the header row and no data.

docs.title: Procedure for one scenario
docs.text:
1. The teacher phone starts a session. Note the teacher phone model.
  2. A student phone goes to a labelled position (front, middle, back, door, corridor, adjacent_room) and checks in.
  3. Record expected (accept inside the room under the policy, reject outside), the claim values, the result from the server, and the latencies.
  4. Repeat for each position with at least two student phone models.

The server also records every accepted and rejected claim in audit_events, which you can cross check against the CSV.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text: Column Meaning run_id Identifier for one scenario run timestamp_utc ISO 8601 time of the attempt teacher_phone, student_phone Device models android_version Version on the student phone room_label Room name position_label front, middle, back, door, corridor, adjacent_room expected accept or reject median_rssi_dbm, sample_count Values sent in the claim result accepted, or the rejection reason discovery_ms, completion_ms Latencies in milliseconds

docs.title: Mahi’s Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024160102 Name: Mahi Singh

  • W1 : Discovery Worked on Android but Not on iPhone
  • W2 : Wireless Debugging Kept Dropping the iPhone
  • W3 : Making Sure the Advertisement Fits
  • W4 : Journals Missing From the Docs Site
  • W5 : Checking the Token the Student Phone Reads

docs.title: Week 1 : Discovery Worked on Android but Not on iPhone
Error:
docs.text: With an iPhone as the teacher, student phones found nothing. There was no error message on either phone.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Each platform had passed its own checks: unit tests, static analysis and a run on a single real phone. The problem only showed once an iPhone acted as the teacher.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The failure followed the teacher phone, not the student. Android teachers were found; the iPhone teacher was not. The session code lived in manufacturer data, a field iOS does not let apps advertise.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Reported the finding to the team. The code now travels in the device name on iPhones (CL plus the digits) and the scanner reads both places. Later the token moved to a Bluetooth read, which works on both.

Because

iOS limits what an app may advertise to a name and service UUIDs, and drops the rest without any error. Only a test across both platforms could catch it.

docs.title: Week 2 : Wireless Debugging Kept Dropping the iPhone
Error:
docs.text: flutter run over Wi Fi to the iPhone kept losing the connection, so test runs stopped halfway.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Testing needs the app installed and running on a real phone, since BLE peripheral mode does not work in the simulator.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The debugger connection was the unstable part, not the app. A release build does not need a debugger attached.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Build in release mode and install it with Apple's device tool:

flutter build ios --release
xcrun devicectl device install app \
  --device <device-id> build/ios/iphoneos/Runner.app

For Android, build the release APK and sideload it:

flutter build apk --release

The Android release APK came to 45 MB.

Because

A release build runs on its own on the phone, so a dropped Wi Fi link no longer ends the test.

docs.title: Week 3 : Making Sure the Advertisement Fits
Error:
docs.text: A change to the advertisement could push it over the BLE size limit, and the phone would then fail to advertise at runtime with no clear message.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
A legacy advertisement holds 31 bytes. On Android the prototype used:

flags                3
128 bit service UUID 18
manufacturer data    10
total                31

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The budget was exactly full, so any extra byte would break it, and nothing checked it before a device test.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Added a unit test so the build fails first:

test('fits a legacy Android advertisement', () {
  const flags = 3;
  const serviceUuid128 = 2 + 16;
  final manufacturerData = 2 + 2 + SessionCode.encode('999999').length;
  expect(flags + serviceUuid128 + manufacturerData,
      lessThanOrEqualTo(31));
});

The prototype ended with 16 unit tests, all passing.

Because

A cheap test that runs on every push catches a size mistake long before anyone carries two phones into a classroom.

docs.title: Week 4 : Journals Missing From the Docs Site
Error:
docs.text: On the docs site the Journals heading showed with no names under it, and the deploy step failed.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
docs/summary.md lists the site navigation:

- Journals
  - [Vemula Manvi Smaran](journals/1024160111-vemula-manvi-smaran/index.md)
  - [Vrishank Nehru](journals/1024160109-vrishank-nehru/index.md)

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The nested items used two spaces. The navigation plugin reads Markdown lists, where a nested item needs four spaces.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Indent the nested items four spaces:

- Journals
    - [Vemula Manvi Smaran](journals/1024160111-vemula-manvi-smaran/index.md)
    - [Vrishank Nehru](journals/1024160109-vrishank-nehru/index.md)

Because

With two spaces the items count as a separate list, so the Journals section had no children and the build failed.

docs.title: Week 5 : Checking the Token the Student Phone Reads
Error:
docs.text: Once the token moved to a Bluetooth read, a student phone could connect to the wrong device, or read before the teacher phone had a token, and get bytes that are not a token. Sending those to the server wastes a request and shows the student a confusing error.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
A real token always has the same shape:

version (1) | session alias (4) | epoch (4) | HMAC tag (8)

17 bytes, and the first byte is the version, 1.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The phone cannot tell whether a token is genuine, only the server can. But it can reject anything with the wrong shape before asking the server.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
A shape check on the phone, plus tests that pin it:

bool looksLikeToken(List<int> bytes) =>
    bytes.length == tokenLength && bytes.first == tokenVersion;

test('recognises the token shape only', () {
  expect(looksLikeToken(token), isTrue);
  expect(looksLikeToken(token.sublist(1)), isFalse);       // too short
  expect(looksLikeToken([2, ...token.sublist(1)]), isFalse); // wrong version
});

test('room code is the session alias in capitals', () {
  expect(roomCodeOf(token), '01020304');
});

The room code test matters too: both phones show those 8 characters, so a student can compare with the teacher's screen.

Because

Cheap checks on the phone catch the common mistakes early with a clear message, and the server still makes the real decision.

docs.title: Vrishank’s Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024160109 Name: Vrishank Nehru

  • W1 : One Stray Reading Marked a Student Present
  • W2 : Check In Blocked on Android 12 and Newer
  • W3 : Student Phone Lost the Teacher Mid Check In
  • W4 : Cancel Did Nothing During a Long Wait
  • W5 : Check In Again Did Not Reset the Scanner

docs.title: Week 1 : One Stray Reading Marked a Student Present
Error:
docs.text: If the app trusted a single Bluetooth reading, a student two rooms away could be marked present: one strong packet would be enough to pass the distance check.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The simplest check compares each reading with the threshold as soon as it arrives:

if (event.rssi >= thresholdDbm) {
  // check in
}

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: RSSI jumps by 10 dBm or more from one packet to the next because of walls, bodies and reflections. A single packet says very little about distance.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Collect every reading over a 4 second window and decide on the median:

int medianRssi(List<int> samples) {
  final sorted = [...samples]..sort();
  final mid = sorted.length ~/ 2;
  if (sorted.length.isOdd) return sorted[mid];
  return ((sorted[mid - 1] + sorted[mid]) / 2).round();
}

The server also asks for a minimum number of samples, 3 by default, so a window with one lucky packet fails.

Because

The median ignores outliers: one reading of −50 dBm among readings near −85 dBm leaves the median near −85, while an average would move.

docs.title: Week 2 : Check In Blocked on Android 12 and Newer
Error:
docs.text: On newer Android phones the student check in never started. The permission step reported a denial even after the user tapped Allow.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The manifest declares the scan permission with the neverForLocation flag, because the app only uses signal strength and never works out a location:

<uses-permission
    android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_SCAN"
    android:usesPermissionFlags="neverForLocation" />

but the app still required ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION before scanning.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: With neverForLocation set, Android 12 and newer auto deny the location request without showing a dialog. A hard requirement on location therefore failed every time.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Treat the Bluetooth permissions as the real requirement, and ask for location only as a best effort for Android 11 and older:

final outcome = await _request(androidPermissions);
if (outcome != PermissionOutcome.granted) return outcome;
// Pre Android 12 needs location for BLE scanning; on newer
// versions this request must not block the session.
await Permission.locationWhenInUse.request();
return PermissionOutcome.granted;

Because

From Android 12, Bluetooth scanning has its own runtime permissions. Location is only needed on older versions, so it cannot be a blocker on new ones.

docs.title: Week 3 : Student Phone Lost the Teacher Mid Check In
Matching Readings to the Right Phone
Error:
docs.text: After reading the token, the student phone could wait until the code expired, reporting too few readings, even while standing next to the teacher.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The check in first finds the teacher phone, reads the token, then scans again and keeps only readings from that same phone:

if (event.peripheral.uuid == teacher.uuid) {
  fromTeacher.add(event.rssi);
}

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Android may advertise from a new random address after a connection or a restart of advertising. The phone was still there, just under a different id, so every reading was thrown away.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Keep two lists. If the matched phone gives nothing for two windows in a row, fall back to readings from any ClassLink teacher in range:

var batch = List<int>.of(fromTeacher);
if (batch.isEmpty) {
  emptyWindows++;
  if (emptyWindows >= 2) batch = List<int>.of(fromAnyTeacher);
}

Because

Bluetooth privacy rotates device addresses on purpose. The scan already filters on the ClassLink service UUID, so any reading it returns comes from a teacher phone.

docs.title: Week 4 : Cancel Did Nothing During a Long Wait
Error:
docs.text: Tapping Cancel while the app searched for a teacher would have no effect until the 60 second search timed out.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The search waited on a future with a timeout:

await firstSighting.future.timeout(_findTimeout);

so a cancel flag checked after that line is seen too late.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A Dart await cannot be interrupted from outside. The code only noticed the flag once the slow future finished.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Race every long wait against a cancel signal:

Future<T> _cancellable<T>(Future<T> future) async {
  final outcome = await Future.any<Object?>([
    future.then<Object?>((value) => _Value<T>(value)),
    _cancelSignal.future.then<Object?>((_) => null),
  ]);
  if (outcome is _Value<T>) return outcome.value;
  throw const _Cancelled();
}

cancel() completes _cancelSignal, so the wait ends at once.

Because

Future.any completes with whichever future finishes first. The slow future keeps running in the background, but nothing waits on it any more.

docs.title: Week 5 : Check In Again Did Not Reset the Scanner
Error:
docs.text: In the prototype, tapping Check In Again after a successful check in did nothing useful. On a second try the student phone sometimes counted old signal readings, and if no teacher was nearby the scan never stopped.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
StudentScanner.startScanning subscribed to the BLE streams every time it ran:

_stateSub = _manager.stateChanged.listen(...);
_discoveredSub = _manager.discovered.listen(_onDiscovered);

and the window timer simply rescheduled itself while no advertisement arrived:

if (_samples.isEmpty) {
  _scheduleWindowEvaluation(name, rollNumber);
  return;
}

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Two things leaked between runs. The old stream subscriptions stayed alive, so a second run had two listeners feeding _samples. And nothing put a limit on how long a scan could last.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Cancel the old subscriptions before starting, and stop after a fixed time:

await _discoveredSub?.cancel();
await _stateSub?.cancel();
_scanStartedAt = DateTime.now();

if (startedAt != null &&
    DateTime.now().difference(startedAt) > maxScanDuration) {
  await _timeOut();   // stops scanning, shows a message
  return;
}

with maxScanDuration set to 90 seconds.

Because

A Dart StreamSubscription keeps delivering events until someone calls cancel(). Starting a new listen does not replace the old one, it adds another.

docs.title: Manvi’s Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024160111 Name: Vemula Manvi Smaran

  • W1 : Signatures Broke on the Observation Time
  • W2 : A Photographed Code Should Not Work Later
  • W3 : One Student Marked Twice
  • W4 : SRS Cover Title Would Not Turn Bold
  • W5 : Release App Pointed at an Empty Server Address

docs.title: Week 1 : Signatures Broke on the Observation Time
Error:
docs.text: A claim signed on the phone would fail the server check with bad_signature, even with the right key and data.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
Both sides build the same text and the phone signs it. The server built the last line from the observation time like this:

parts = [
    CLAIM_DOMAIN, str(session_id), str(nonce),
    token_hex.lower(), str(median_rssi), str(sample_count),
    observed_at.isoformat(),
]

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: isoformat() is not the same string in every language. Python writes 2026-10-15T12:00:00+00:00, while Dart writes 2026-10-15T12:00:00.000Z, and fractions of a second appear or vanish. One different character means a different signature.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Sign whole seconds since the Unix epoch instead:

# Whole seconds since the Unix epoch: identical in every
# language, unlike ISO 8601.
str(int(observed_at.timestamp())),

and pin it with a shared golden vector that both the Python and the Dart tests check:

classlink-claim-v1
11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555
aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-eeeeeeeeeeee
0101020304000000f1a1b2c3d4e5f60708
-62
5
1792065600

Because

A signature covers exact bytes, not meaning. Two strings that mean the same moment still fail if any byte differs, so the format must have only one way to write it.

docs.title: Week 2 : A Photographed Code Should Not Work Later
Error:
docs.text: In the prototype the session code stayed the same for the whole class. A student could send it to a friend outside the room, and the friend could check in.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The server now issues the token the teacher phone shares:

version (1) | session alias (4) | epoch (4) | HMAC tag (8)

17 bytes in total. The epoch is the current 15 second period.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Making the code change is not enough on its own, because anyone could invent a code. The server has to be able to tell that it made the code, and when.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
The tag is an HMAC over the version, alias, epoch and session id, keyed with a secret only the server holds:

def _tag(secret, session_id, alias, epoch):
    message = struct.pack(">B4sI", TOKEN_VERSION, alias, epoch) + session_id.bytes
    return hmac.new(secret, message, hashlib.sha256).digest()[:8]

and a token is only fresh within a small window:

def epoch_is_fresh(token_epoch, now_epoch, grace_epochs):
    return now_epoch - grace_epochs <= token_epoch <= now_epoch + 1

Because

Without the secret nobody can make a valid tag, and with one epoch of grace a code stops working about 30 seconds after it was on air. A forwarded code is stale before a friend can use it.

docs.title: Error:
docs.text: When a phone retried a claim after a slow network reply, the server could accept the same one time code twice, or record two rows for the same student.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: Accepting a claim does two writes: mark the challenge as used, then insert the attendance row. Done as two separate steps, two requests arriving together could both pass the "not used yet" check.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The check and the write must happen as one step inside the database, not in Python.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Do both writes in one transaction and let the database decide:

update challenges set used_at = %s
 where id = %s and used_at is null
 returning id;

insert into attendance (...)
values (...)
on conflict (session_id, student_id) do nothing
returning *;

If the update returns nothing, another request already used the code; if the insert returns nothing, the student is already present. A genuine retry gets the stored record back with duplicate_retry: true.

Because

used_at is null in the where clause makes the update claim the row atomically: only one request can flip it. The unique key on (session_id, student_id) does the same for attendance.

docs.title: Week 4 : SRS Cover Title Would Not Turn Bold
Error:
docs.text: On the SRS cover page the very large title came out in a light weight, and stopped growing past a certain size, so it did not match the template screenshot.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The document loads T1 font encoding, and the cover used:

\bfseries
{\Huge SOFTWARE REQUIREMENTS\\SPECIFICATION}

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Two limits met here. In T1 encoding the bold face at that size was not installed, so LaTeX swapped in a regular one. OT1 does have bold Computer Modern, but its sizes stop at 24.88pt (\Huge), so asking for more changes nothing.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Switch the cover alone to OT1 for the bold shapes, keep \Huge, and scale the whole block up instead of asking for a bigger font size:

\begin{titlepage}
  \fontencoding{OT1}\selectfont
  \scalebox{1.17}{\begin{minipage}{5.85in}
    \begin{flushright}\bfseries
      {\Huge SOFTWARE REQUIREMENTS\\SPECIFICATION}
      ...

Because

LaTeX picks a font by encoding, family, series and size. If that exact combination is missing it falls back quietly and only prints a warning in the log.

docs.title: Week 5 : Release App Pointed at an Empty Server Address
Error:
docs.text: A release APK built in GitHub Actions without the server variable set would try to call an empty address instead of the local fallback.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The workflow passes the address into the build:

flutter build apk --release \
  --dart-define=API_BASE_URL="$API_BASE_URL"

and the app read it with a default:

const String.fromEnvironment(
  'API_BASE_URL',
  defaultValue: 'http://10.0.2.2:8000',
)

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: When the variable is unset, the shell still passes API_BASE_URL= with an empty value. The define exists, so defaultValue never applies.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Treat empty the same as missing:

apiBaseUrl: _trimSlash(
  const String.fromEnvironment('API_BASE_URL').isEmpty
      ? localApi
      : const String.fromEnvironment('API_BASE_URL'),
),

and print a warning in the workflow when the variable is not set.

Because

String.fromEnvironment falls back only when the name was never defined. An empty string counts as defined.

docs.title: Khagendra’s Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024160123 Name: Khagendra Saini

  • W1 : Sending the Session Code From an iPhone
  • W2 : Bluetooth Calls Failed Right After Launch on iPhone
  • W3 : Back Button Silently Stopped Attendance
  • W4 : Keyboard Covered the Correction Form
  • W5 : An iPhone Could Not Share the Session Token

docs.title: Week 1 : Sending the Session Code From an iPhone
Error:
docs.text: An iPhone teacher advertised, but student phones never saw the session code.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The prototype put the code in manufacturer data:

manufacturerSpecificData: [
  ManufacturerSpecificData(
    id: BleConstants.manufacturerId,
    data: SessionCode.encode(_sessionCode!),
  ),
],

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: iOS lets an app advertise only a local name and service UUIDs. Manufacturer data is dropped without an error. On Android the opposite care is needed: setting a name renames the phone itself.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Choose the field by platform:

name: Platform.isIOS
    ? SessionCode.toAdvertisedName(_sessionCode!) // CL042917
    : null,
manufacturerSpecificData: Platform.isIOS ? [] : [...],

and let the scanner read either one:

_detectedSessionCode =
    (matches.isNotEmpty ? SessionCode.decode(matches.first.data) : null) ??
    SessionCode.fromAdvertisedName(event.advertisement.name);

Because

One scanner that checks both places finds an Android or an iPhone teacher without knowing which one it is.

docs.title: Week 2 : Bluetooth Calls Failed Right After Launch on iPhone
Error:
docs.text: On a fresh launch the iPhone could fail to start scanning or advertising, because the app sent Bluetooth commands before the phone's Bluetooth was ready.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The app called the BLE manager as soon as the screen opened:

await _manager.startAdvertising(advertisement);

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: CoreBluetooth starts in the unknown state and only later reports poweredOn. It rejects commands sent before that.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Wait for the state to settle, with a timeout, and give a clear message for each problem:

Future<void> waitForPoweredOn(BluetoothLowEnergyManager m) async {
  var state = m.state;
  if (state == BluetoothLowEnergyState.unknown) {
    state = await m.stateChanged
        .map((e) => e.state)
        .firstWhere((s) => s != BluetoothLowEnergyState.unknown)
        .timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5));
  }
  if (state == BluetoothLowEnergyState.poweredOff) {
    throw const BluetoothUnavailableException(
      'Bluetooth is off. Turn it on in Settings or Control Centre and try again.');
  }
  // unauthorized and unsupported get their own messages
}

Because

The Bluetooth stack powers up asynchronously. Waiting for the state event is the only reliable way to know it is ready.

docs.title: Week 3 : Back Button Silently Stopped Attendance
Error:
docs.text: A teacher who pressed Back during class would leave the session screen, which stops the Bluetooth broadcast. Students could no longer check in, and nothing warned the teacher.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: The teacher phone only shares the token while the session screen is open; leaving it disposes the broadcaster.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Leaving the screen is a big action that looked like a small one. It needed a confirmation step.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Wrap the screen in PopScope and ask first:

PopScope(
  canPop: false,
  onPopInvokedWithResult: (didPop, _) async {
    if (didPop) return;
    final navigator = Navigator.of(context);
    if (await _confirmLeave()) navigator.pop();
  },
  child: ...,
)

The dialog offers Keep running or End session; ending also closes the session on the server.

Because

canPop: false stops the system back gesture, so the screen decides what Back means while a class is live.

docs.title: Week 4 : Keyboard Covered the Correction Form
Error:
docs.text: When a teacher types the reason for a correction, the keyboard would cover the text field and the Save correction button.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The correction form opens in a bottom sheet:

showModalBottomSheet<(bool, String)>(
  context: context,
  builder: (_) => _CorrectionSheet(row: row),
);

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A bottom sheet does not move up for the keyboard by default. It also has a height limit unless told otherwise.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Let the sheet take the space it needs and pad it by the keyboard height:

showModalBottomSheet(
  context: context,
  isScrollControlled: true,
  builder: (_) => _CorrectionSheet(row: row),
);

Padding(
  padding: EdgeInsets.fromLTRB(
    24, 24, 24, 24 + MediaQuery.of(context).viewInsets.bottom,
  ),
  ...
)

Because

viewInsets.bottom is the height the keyboard takes up. Adding it as padding keeps the field and the button above the keyboard.

docs.title: Week 5 : An iPhone Could Not Share the Session Token
Error:
docs.text: The server token is 17 bytes, and an iPhone teacher had no way to put it in a Bluetooth advertisement. iOS only lets apps advertise a name and service UUIDs, and a name long enough for 17 bytes does not fit either.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: A legacy BLE advertisement holds 31 bytes. The 128 bit service UUID alone takes 18 of them. The earlier fix, the code in the device name, worked for a 6 digit code but not for a 17 byte signed token.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The advertisement only needs to say "a ClassLink teacher is here". The token can travel another way once the student has found the phone.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
The teacher phone advertises only the service UUID and serves the token from a readable characteristic:

GATTCharacteristic.mutable(
  uuid: BleConstants.tokenCharacteristicUuid,
  properties: [GATTCharacteristicProperty.read],
  permissions: [GATTCharacteristicPermission.read],
  descriptors: [],
);

and answers each read with the latest token from the server:

await _manager.respondReadRequestWithValue(
  event.request,
  value: token.sublist(offset),
);

Because

A GATT read has no 31 byte limit and CoreBluetooth allows it, so an iPhone can now be the teacher phone, the same as an Android one.

docs.title: Software Requirements Specification
docs.text:
ClassLink: A BLE Based Classroom Attendance System

Version 1.0, October 2026. UCS503P Software Engineering Project, Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology.

Prepared by Vemula Manvi Smaran (1024160111), Vrishank Nehru (1024160109), Mahi Singh (1024160102), and Khagendra Saini (1024160123). Submitted to Anushka Ma'am.

The glossary, API summary, rejection codes, evaluation plan, test traceability, and two more diagrams live in the supplement.

docs.title: 1.1 Purpose
docs.text:
Taking attendance by roll call eats lecture time, and a signed sheet or a shouted "present" is easy to fake and hard to check later. ClassLink is the fix. It is a classroom attendance system where the teacher's phone broadcasts a short lived Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) token, each student's phone hears it and sends a signed claim, and a server decides who counts as present. The main idea is that the phone never decides for itself, so the record can be trusted.

This document is the Software Requirements Specification (SRS) of ClassLink Version 1.0. It follows the approved project proposal (UCS503P). Requirements carry an ID such as FR (functional) and a priority from the MoSCoW scheme: Must (needed for the pilot), Should (next iteration), Could (optional). A Status column says what is built today.

docs.title: 1.2 Intended Audience and Reading Suggestions
docs.text:
This SRS is for developers, testers, pilot teachers, and the course instructor. It gives the internal, external, functional, and nonfunctional details of ClassLink. Every requirement is written so a test can check it.

Key terms used in this document:

  • BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy): the short range radio the phones use. It needs no pairing.
  • Token: a 17 byte code the teacher phone broadcasts. It changes every 15 seconds and names no person.
  • Challenge (nonce): a one time code the server gives a student before a check in, so nobody can reuse an old claim.
  • Claim: the signed message a student phone sends. It holds the one time code, token, signal strength, sample count, and time.
  • RSSI: received signal strength in dBm. A larger number (closer to zero) means a closer phone.
  • Session: one class period in which attendance is open.
  • Device key: the signing key kept on a student's phone. The server stores only its public half.
  • Audit log: the server's permanent record of who did what.
  • POC: the earlier offline proof of concept app.

docs.title: 1.3 Project Scope
docs.text:
ClassLink gives Teachers and Students one place to run attendance, and gives the Administrator control over who may teach. It records presence only. It does not grade, schedule, or track location.

Objectives.

  1. Speed: a student checks in within 10 seconds of starting the scan, so roll call stops costing lecture time.
  2. Trust: the server verifies every claim, so a phone cannot mark itself present.
  3. Traceability: every claim, rejection, and correction leaves a record.
  4. Teacher control: a live roster, manual corrections with a reason, and CSV export.
  5. Privacy: the system keeps only name, roll number, email, a device public key, and attendance. It never collects location.
  6. Engineering quality: the backend passes Ruff and strict MyPy, and every requirement marked Done has an automated test run in CI.

In scope. Teacher and student roles on Android and iOS, built from one Flutter code base. Classrooms with join codes. One registered phone per student. Attendance sessions with a signal strength rule. A live roster, manual corrections, and CSV export. An audit log. Testing on real phones in a real room.

Optional extensions (outside this course submission). Links to learning management systems, and a signal threshold that adapts to each room.

Out of scope. Proving that the phone's owner is the person holding it. Student to student relaying. Grading and timetables.

Status terms. Done means built and covered by an automated test. POC means present only in the offline proof of concept. Planned means specified but not built. Today the server side is built and tested. The mobile apps (Android and iOS) do not call it yet, so anything that needs an app is Planned.

Stakeholders.

Stakeholder Role Main interest Students Join classrooms, register a phone, check in A quick check in that counts Teachers Create classrooms, run sessions, correct records Accurate attendance without roll call Administrator Sets up the server, edits the approved teacher list A secure, running system Development team Design, build, test, deploy Clear, testable requirements Course instructor Reviews and evaluates the project Consistency with the approved proposal Supabase Hosts the database and sign in Fair use of its free tier

Table: Stakeholders of ClassLink.

Figure 1.1 is the overview of the project. A Teacher creates a Classroom. The Classroom runs a Session. The Session issues rotating Tokens. A Student hears a Token and signs a Claim. The server checks the Claim into an Attendance record, and the Teacher sees it in the Roster and CSV. Every entity feeds the next one, so the whole system works as one chain.

docs.title: 2.1 Product Perspective
docs.text:
ClassLink grew from an offline proof of concept, the Flutter app in code/, that showed a teacher phone can announce a session over BLE and a student phone can check in by proximity. Version 1.0 adds a server so the result no longer depends on trusting the student's phone. It follows a layered client and server design (Figure 2.1).

  • Mobile app: Flutter, for Android and iOS, with a teacher mode and a student mode.
  • Backend API: FastAPI (Python) for sign in checks, validation, sessions, and claims.
  • Business logic: rotating tokens, claim checks, corrections, and export.
  • Database: Supabase Postgres. Supabase Auth signs users in.

One check in works like this. The teacher app fetches a fresh token from the server every 15 seconds and broadcasts it. A student phone hears the token and asks the server for a one time challenge. The phone measures signal strength for a few seconds, signs the result with its own key, and sends it. The server verifies the claim and records attendance.

docs.title: 2.2 User Classes and Characteristics
docs.text:
ClassLink has four user classes (Figure 2.2).

  • Teacher. Runs sessions for classrooms they own. The role comes only from a list of approved teacher emails kept by the administrator.
  • Student. Joins classrooms with a join code and checks in with one registered phone.
  • Administrator. Sets up the server and edits the approved teacher list. This is not an in app role.
  • Evaluator. Reads the exported CSV files. No app access needed.

Supabase Auth is the one external system. It signs users in and issues their tokens.

Students and teachers need only basic phone skills. The administrator needs medium technical skill.

docs.title: 2.3 Product Functions
docs.text:
ClassLink stores classrooms, sessions, and attendance, and keeps a record of every important action. At a high level it lets users sign in and get a role, create or join a classroom, register a device key, start and end sessions with rotating tokens, check in with a signed claim, watch a live roster, correct mistakes with a reason, and export a CSV. Users must sign in before using any of these functions.

The main data records are:

  • profiles: user id, role (teacher or student), full name, roll number, email.
  • classrooms: classroom id, teacher id, name, unique join code.
  • enrollments: classroom id and student id, with the join time.
  • devices: student id, public key, label, time it was cancelled. A student has one active device.
  • sessions: classroom id, alias, signal threshold, sample window, minimum samples, start and end time. A classroom has at most one active session.
  • challenges: session id, student id, token, issue and expiry time, used time. Each is single use.
  • attendance: session id, student id, status, source (BLE claim or manual correction), median RSSI, sample count, time of measurement, and correction details. One record per student per session.
  • audit_events: actor, action, subject, details, time.

Links between the tables keep the data consistent. The level 0 diagram (Figure 2.3) treats ClassLink as one box and shows what crosses its edge. Arrows pointing right mean data going in. Arrows pointing left mean data coming out.

Level 1 (Figure 2.4) opens the box into six processes. Each process keeps its data in a store, drawn under it.

docs.title: 2.4 Operating Environment
docs.text:
Students and teachers use an Android phone (8.0 or later) or an iPhone, both with Bluetooth LE. The lowest iOS version is still to be confirmed. The teacher phone must support BLE advertising, so we test on real phones of both kinds. The server runs in a Linux container behind HTTPS. The database is Supabase Postgres. Phones need internet during check in, but the Bluetooth exchange itself does not.

External interfaces.

  • User interface: a Flutter app with a teacher mode (classrooms, session control, live roster, corrections, export) and a student mode (join, register phone, check in, result). Every rejection shows a plain explanation.
  • Hardware: Bluetooth LE radio. The teacher phone needs BLE advertising. No other hardware.
  • Software: FastAPI backend, Supabase Postgres, Supabase Auth, GitHub Actions for CI.
  • Communications: HTTPS with JSON over REST. A Supabase sign in token (JWT) in the Authorization header. A 17 byte token inside the BLE advertisement.

Design and implementation constraints.

  • Stack: Flutter (Android and iOS), FastAPI on Python 3.11 or later, psycopg 3, Supabase Postgres and Auth.
  • A phone never creates an attendance record on its own. Only the server decides.
  • Secrets stay on the server. Only .env.example files enter the repository.
  • The BLE token is 17 bytes and travels in the manufacturer data field of the BLE advertisement, because a service identifier plus the token does not fit in a basic one. We have not yet confirmed this layout on phones. iOS does not allow manufacturer data in an advertisement. The proof of concept handles this by sending its 6 digit session code in the advertised device name on iPhones (CL plus the digits) and in manufacturer data on Android, and the student scanner reads both. Version 1.0 must fit its 17 byte token into the same two routes, and we have not yet confirmed that it fits.
  • Apps write only through the API. The database gives apps read only access to their own rows.
  • Four person team, one semester, with the work split across backend, app, documentation, and testing.

Assumptions and dependencies.

  • Students use the phone they registered. A student who changes phones registers again.
  • Phone and server clocks stay within about a minute.
  • Supabase free tier limits are enough for the pilot.
  • Signal strength is noisy, so the server uses the median of several samples against a per session threshold. The right threshold is tuned on real phones.

docs.title: 2.5 Design
docs.text:
A check in follows the flow in Figure 2.5. It crosses three places: the teacher app, the server, and the student app.

Student activities have three steps: join a classroom, register the phone once, and check in. Everything ends in the student's profile (Figure 2.6).

Teacher activities (Figure 2.7) cover setting up a classroom, running a session, and keeping the records straight.

The administrator has one small job. They keep the server running and decide who is a teacher (Figure 2.8).

Figure 2.9 shows every use case and who starts it.

UC-1 Check in to a session. Actor: student, who must be signed in, enrolled, and have a registered phone. The teacher has a session running. The student taps Check in. The app scans for the token for the sample window and requests a challenge. The server checks the token, session, enrollment, and device, then issues a one time code. The app signs the claim and sends it. The server checks the one time code, signature, time, sample count, and median signal, then records attendance and shows Present. If the signal is weak or samples are too few, the student sees a plain message and may move closer and retry. Any other failure shows its reason code and nothing is recorded.

UC-2 Correct attendance. Actor: teacher, who owns the classroom. The teacher opens the roster, picks a student, and marks them present or absent with a reason of at least five characters. The server stores the change with the teacher's name and writes an audit event. A reason that is too short is refused and nothing changes.

The design rules behind these flows:

  • Teacher broadcasts, student listens. There is no relay between students.
  • The server decides. Every claim is checked on the server.
  • Real data only. Evaluation figures come only from recorded real runs.

docs.title: 3. System Features
docs.text: ClassLink is a classroom attendance system. The main part of this product is to accept a signed BLE claim and decide on the server whether it counts.

docs.title: 3.1 Description and Priority
docs.text:
ClassLink has main features and some sub features. In priority order, from top to bottom:

  1. Attendance claims (Must, pilot): challenge, signed claim, server checks. This is the goal feature of the software.
  2. Sessions and tokens (Must, pilot): start and end sessions, rotating BLE token.
  3. Device binding (Must, pilot): one registered key per student.
  4. Accounts and classrooms (Must, pilot): sign in, roles, join codes.
  5. Roster and corrections (Must, pilot): live list, fixes with a reason.
  6. Export and audit (Should): CSV download and audit log.
  7. Offline mode (Could): the original no server demo, labelled as not the official record.

The first meaningful milestone is a working pilot where a teacher starts a session, a student checks in from a real phone, and the roster shows the result. The server side of this is done. The app side is planned.

docs.title: 3.2 Functional Requirements
docs.text:
The server is a FastAPI service built and tested against a real Postgres. The app still needs its API client, sign in, key storage, token broadcast, and roster screens. Priority is Must, Should, or Could. The Status column marks what is built.

Accounts and classrooms

ID Requirement Priority Status FR-ACC-01 The API shall accept only requests with a valid, unexpired Supabase token and answer all others with HTTP 401. Must Done FR-ACC-02 A user shall have one profile with the role teacher or student. Only emails on the approved teacher list become teachers. A student profile shall require a roll number. Must Done FR-ACC-03 Students shall not reach teacher operations, and teachers shall not reach student operations (HTTP 403). Must Done FR-CLS-01 A teacher shall create a classroom and receive a unique six character join code. Must Done FR-CLS-02 A student shall join a classroom with its code. An unknown code shall return HTTP 404. Must Done

Device binding

ID Requirement Priority Status FR-DEV-01 A student shall register one device key (ECDSA P-256 public key). The server shall reject any other key type. Must Done FR-DEV-02 Registering a new key shall cancel the old one and write an audit event. Must Done FR-DEV-03 The private key shall never leave the phone (kept in the Android Keystore or the iOS Keychain), and the app shall sign only after fingerprint, face, or screen lock authentication. Must Planned

Sessions and tokens

ID Requirement Priority Status FR-SES-01 A teacher shall start a session for their own classroom with a signal threshold (default −75 dBm), a sample window (default 4 s), and a minimum sample count (default 3). A classroom shall have at most one active session. Must Done FR-SES-02 A teacher shall end a session. After that the server shall reject its tokens, challenges, and claims. Must Done FR-SES-03 The server shall issue a 17 byte rotating token that changes every 15 seconds and carries no student or teacher identity. Must Done FR-SES-04 Only the classroom's teacher shall see or change its sessions. Other teachers shall get HTTP 404. Must Done FR-SES-05 The teacher app shall fetch a fresh token each period and broadcast it. Must Planned FR-SES-06 On iOS the teacher app shall broadcast the token through a route iOS allows, such as the advertised device name used in the proof of concept. If the 17 byte token cannot fit, the document shall say that an Android phone must act as the teacher device. Should Planned

Attendance claims

ID Requirement Priority Status FR-ATT-01 The student app shall scan for the token and collect signal strength samples. Must Planned FR-ATT-02 On a challenge request the server shall check the token, the active session, enrollment, and the student's registered device, then issue a one time code (nonce) valid for 120 seconds. Must Done FR-ATT-03 A claim shall hold the one time code, token, median signal strength, sample count, and time of measurement (whole seconds), signed with the device key over a fixed text format. Must Done FR-ATT-04 The server shall accept a claim only if the one time code is the caller's, unused, and unexpired, the token matches, the signature verifies, the time of measurement is within 60 seconds of server time, the sample count meets the minimum, and the median signal meets the threshold. Must Done FR-ATT-05 A student shall have at most one attendance record per session. Repeating an accepted claim shall return the same record. Must Done FR-ATT-06 A weak signal or too few samples shall leave the one time code usable so the student can move closer and retry. Should Done FR-ATT-07 Every rejection shall carry a reason code (listed in the supplement) with HTTP 409. Must Done FR-ATT-08 The student app shall show the result and explain each reason in plain words. Must Planned

Roster, corrections, export, audit

ID Requirement Priority Status FR-ROS-01 A teacher shall see every enrolled student of a session with status, source, signal strength, and time. Must Done FR-ROS-02 The teacher app shall refresh the roster at least every 5 seconds during a session. Should Planned FR-COR-01 A teacher shall mark a student present or absent with a reason of at least five characters. The server shall audit each correction. Must Done FR-EXP-01 A teacher shall download a session as CSV with every enrolled student. The export shall make safe any cell that starts with =, +, -, or @. Must Done FR-AUD-01 The server shall audit classroom creation, device binding, session start and end, accepted and rejected claims, corrections, and exports. Apps shall have no access to the audit log. Must Done FR-POC-01 The original offline mode shall remain and be labelled as not the official record. Could POC

docs.title: 4.1 Performance Requirements
docs.text:
These are targets. We report only values measured in the pilot.

  • Discovery: a student phone shall pick up the token within 5 seconds in the same room.
  • Check in: from scan start to server result within 10 seconds.
  • API: p95 under 500 ms for challenge and claim calls with 50 students at once.
  • Capacity: one classroom of 300 students with up to 150 check ins at once.

docs.title: 4.2 Security Requirements
docs.text:
• All traffic shall use HTTPS in production.
  • Secrets, such as the token key and database credentials, shall exist only on the server. CI shall fail if a .env file or keystore is committed.
  • The database shall have row level security on every table, so each user sees only their own rows. Apps read but never write.
  • A signed claim shall cover the session, one time code, token, signal strength, sample count, and time, so changing any value breaks the signature.
  • The server shall compare token tags with a timing safe method, and check every request's sign in token for its signature, expiry, and intended use.
  • The system shall store only name, roll number, email, a device public key, and attendance. It shall not collect location.

ClassLink stops casual proxy attendance (a friend marking you present). It does not stop a friend who holds the student's unlocked phone, or someone who relays a live token to a faraway phone within its few seconds of life. Short token periods, the signal rule, and the audit log reduce these risks but do not remove them.

docs.title: 4.3 Software Quality Attributes
docs.text:
• Reliability: attendance writes happen fully or not at all, so a retry is safe. If two claims for one student arrive together, only one record is made.
  • Availability: the pages /healthz and /readyz report whether the server and database are working.
  • Maintainability: the backend passes Ruff and strict MyPy in CI, and every Done requirement has an automated test.
  • Portability: the server runs from one ready to run package (a container image) and is set up with environment variables.
  • Usability: a student checks in with one tap, and every rejection has a plain explanation.

Acceptance criteria.

Metric Target Discovery A phone picks up the token within 5 seconds in the same room Check in time Scan start to server result within 10 seconds API speed p95 under 500 ms for challenge and claim calls with 50 students at once Functional completeness All Must requirements demonstrated end to end on real phones Test coverage Every requirement marked Done has an automated test that passes in CI Secret safety CI fails if a .env file or keystore is committed Honest results Pilot figures come only from recorded real runs

Table: Acceptance criteria.

docs.title: 4.4 Business Rules
docs.text:
• A student has at most one attendance record per session.
  • Only a classroom's teacher can see or change its attendance.
  • A manual correction always has a reason and a named teacher.
  • An ended session never restarts. A new session gets new tokens.
  • A student has one active phone. Replacing it cancels the old key.
  • Only the administrator decides who becomes a teacher.

docs.title: 5. Other Requirements
docs.text:
ClassLink needs maintenance after the course, because phones, Android and iOS versions, and BLE behaviour keep changing. Other requirements are:

  • Documentation: the repository holds this SRS in Markdown and LaTeX, the project proposal, UML diagrams, the deployment runbook, and the API reference served at /docs.
  • Deployment: the server is packaged as a container that does not run as an admin user, and it refuses to start in production without its database address and secrets. The administrator runs the database setup file on Supabase before the first start. GitHub Actions runs the app and server checks and rejects committed secrets. The team publishes a signed Android APK and an iOS build for the pilot. How the iOS build reaches testers is still to be decided. See docs/deployment.md.
  • Privacy: pilot participants learn what the app stores before they join a classroom. Deleting a user deletes their profile, enrollments, devices, and attendance. English only in the first version.
  • Phasing: Phase 1 (done): server, database schema, tests, CI, and documents. Phase 2 (planned): Android and iOS apps with sign in, key storage, token broadcast, scan and claim, and roster screens. Phase 3 (planned): pilot on real phones in a real room, with measured results. Extensions follow only after the pilot.
  • Open issues to confirm: whether the 17 byte token fits the BLE advertisement on real Android and iOS phones, and whether the token fits the route iOS allows for an iPhone teacher (the advertised device name); the signal threshold that works in a real room; whether to move the sign in token from a shared secret to public key signing; the Android application id, which still carries the old proof of concept name; and the consent wording for pilot students.

Risks and mitigations.

Risk What we do Some phones cannot advertise BLE, and iOS limits what an advert can hold Reuse the proof of concept's two routes (device name on iOS, manufacturer data on Android), test the 17 byte token on real phones early, and fall back to an Android teacher phone if it does not fit Signal strength varies by room and phone Median of several samples, a per session threshold, and a manual correction path A friend relays a live token Short token life, one time code, the signal rule, and the audit log Server or database downtime Health endpoints, a single container image, and managed Postgres Leaked secrets Secrets only on the server, and a CI check that rejects committed ones Scope creep Keep extensions out of the pilot, and track status in Section 3.2

References. (1) ClassLink Project Proposal, UCS503P, Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology. (2) IEEE Std 830-1998, Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications. (3) Supabase and FastAPI documentation.

docs.title: ClassLink SRS Supplement
docs.text: This supplement belongs to the Software Requirements Specification. It holds reference material that would crowd the main document.

docs.title: A. Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning BLE Bluetooth Low Energy RSSI Received signal strength indicator, in dBm. Closer devices read less negative values Epoch A fixed length time slice used to rotate tokens Alias Four random bytes that identify a live session in a token Challenge A single use nonce the server issues after validating a token Claim A signed statement from a student device that it observed a valid token RLS Row level security in Postgres JWT JSON Web Token issued by Supabase Auth SPKI SubjectPublicKeyInfo, the DER format for public keys

docs.title: B. API Summary
docs.text: Method and path Role Purpose POST /v1/profile any user Create the caller's profile GET /v1/me any Read the caller's profile POST /v1/classrooms teacher Create a classroom GET /v1/classrooms any List own classrooms POST /v1/classrooms/join student Join with a join code PUT /v1/devices/me student Bind a device signing key POST /v1/sessions teacher Start a session POST /v1/sessions/{id}/end teacher End a session GET /v1/sessions/{id}/token teacher Current rotating token GET /v1/sessions/{id}/roster teacher Live roster POST /v1/sessions/{id}/corrections teacher Manual correction GET /v1/sessions/{id}/export.csv teacher CSV export POST /v1/attendance/challenge student Trade a token for a nonce POST /v1/attendance/claim student Submit a signed claim GET /healthz, GET /readyz none Liveness and readiness

docs.title: C. Rejection Reasons
docs.text:
The API returns HTTP 409 with {"status": "rejected", "reason": "<code>"}.

Code Meaning Stage invalid_token Malformed token or wrong tag challenge token_expired Token epoch outside the grace window challenge session_not_active Unknown alias or ended session challenge, claim not_enrolled Student is not in the classroom challenge no_device_bound Student has no active device key challenge, claim challenge_unknown Nonce missing or issued to someone else claim challenge_expired Nonce older than 120 seconds claim nonce_reused Nonce consumed by a different claim claim token_mismatch Claim token differs from the challenge token claim bad_signature Signature does not verify against the active key claim claim_stale Observation time more than 60 seconds from server time claim too_few_samples Sample count below the session minimum claim rssi_below_threshold Median RSSI weaker than the session threshold claim duplicate The student already has a record in this session claim

docs.title: D. Evaluation Plan and Data Schema
docs.text:
Primary metric. Detection success rate: the fraction of labelled position scan attempts (front, middle, back, door, corridor, adjacent room) that accept or reject correctly under the configured policy.

Secondary metrics. Discovery latency, attendance completion latency, false accept and false reject rates at out of room and in room positions, API p50 and p95 latency, and the rejection rate for duplicate claims and expired tokens.

Method. One teacher phone and at least two student phones of different models, in a real classroom. Record raw rows before computing any summary.

Raw CSV schema (docs/evaluation/*.csv):

Column Meaning run_id Identifier for one scenario run timestamp_utc ISO 8601 time of the attempt teacher_phone, student_phone Device models os_version Android or iOS version on the student phone room_label Room name position_label front, middle, back, door, corridor, adjacent_room expected accept or reject median_rssi_dbm, sample_count Values sent in the claim result accepted or the rejection reason discovery_ms, completion_ms Latencies

docs.title: E. Test Traceability
docs.text:
Backend tests live in backend/tests/ and run against a real Postgres.

Requirements Tests FR-ACC-01 to FR-ACC-03, FR-CLS-01, FR-CLS-02, FR-DEV-01, FR-DEV-02 test_teacher_and_accounts.py, test_attendance_flow.py FR-SES-01 to FR-SES-04 test_tokens.py, test_teacher_and_accounts.py FR-ATT-02 to FR-ATT-07 test_attendance_flow.py, test_claims.py, test_crypto.py FR-ROS-01, FR-COR-01, FR-EXP-01, FR-AUD-01 test_teacher_and_accounts.py, test_attendance_flow.py, test_rls.py Row level security, signed claim coverage, atomic writes (Section 4) test_rls.py, test_attendance_flow.py

Requirements marked Planned have no automated test yet. The Flutter unit tests live in code/test/.

docs.title: ClassLink UML Diagrams
docs.text:
This folder contains the UML diagrams for the ClassLink project report. They describe the current BLE proof of concept (POC) that exists in this repository today, plus a small number of clearly separated future / planned elements that are called out visually (dashed borders, red fill, "Not Implemented" labels) and in notes on each diagram.

Every diagram in this folder represents the current POC, except elements that are explicitly labelled "Future", "Planned" or "Not Implemented." No diagram claims the backend, database, authentication, device binding, biometrics, audit logging, or server-side attendance records exist — those are target architecture, not delivered code.

docs.title: What "current POC" actually means
docs.text:
• Teacher phone: BLE peripheral/advertiser, one active session at a time.
  • Student phone: BLE central/scanner, one-hop only (no mesh, no relay).
  • Session identity: a locally generated 6-digit code, carried in Android manufacturer-specific advertisement data, or in the iOS advertised local name as CLXXXXXX (iOS peripherals cannot advertise manufacturer data).
  • Proximity check: 4 seconds of RSSI sampling, median RSSI compared against an experimental -75 dBm threshold.
  • Check-in: a brief GATT connection from student to teacher, one write of a JSON payload containing name and roll number, then disconnect.
  • Attendance is held in memory on the teacher's device for the active session and exported to CSV locally. There is no server, no database, and no cross-device sync.

docs.title: Diagram descriptions
docs.text: # Diagram What it shows 1 Use Case Teacher and student actions available in the POC app, and how they relate (start session includes generating a code and advertising; scanning includes discovery, code reading, and RSSI collection). 2 Class The client-side Flutter classes involved in advertising, scanning, session-code transport, proximity evaluation, and check-in. Not a database schema. 3 Sequence The full student check-in exchange over BLE, including the Android manufacturer-data path, the iOS local-name fallback, an invalid-code branch, a weak-RSSI rejection branch, and the successful check-in branch. 4 Activity The student's step-by-step flow from opening student mode through permission checks, scanning, RSSI evaluation, entering details, and GATT write, with every failure branch shown. 5 Component The Flutter app's layered architecture (presentation, application, BLE communication, native platform, dev/quality tooling), with the planned backend shown as a separate, disconnected, dashed package. 6 Deployment The two physical phones, the private GitHub repository, and the build artifacts (Android APK, iOS device install) used for testing today, with the planned cloud deployment shown as a separate, disconnected, dashed package. 7 State The teacher's session lifecycle state machine, from idle through Bluetooth checks, code generation, advertising, receiving check-ins, and closing the session.

The class diagram (02-class-current-poc.puml) uses conceptual class names chosen for readability in the report. The actual Dart source groups some of that behaviour into fewer files. Mapping:

docs.title: Rendering commands
docs.text:
Diagrams were rendered with PlantUML (plantuml.jar) using Graphviz (dot) for the layered component/deployment layouts. From docs/uml/source/:

# PNG at 300 DPI
java -Dplantuml.dpi=300 -jar plantuml.jar -tpng -o ../png *.puml

Requirements: a JRE (Java 11+) and Graphviz (dot on PATH) — install with brew install graphviz on macOS, or apt-get install graphviz on Linux. Diagrams that use package/node grouping (component and deployment) will render with a degraded layout, or fail, without Graphviz installed.

To render a single diagram:

java -Dplantuml.dpi=300 -jar plantuml.jar -tpng -o ../png 05-component-current-poc.puml

docs.title: Inserting into the report (LaTeX / Overleaf)
docs.text:
1. Ensure main.tex has \usepackage{graphicx} and \usepackage{float} in its preamble (the figures use the [H] placement specifier).
  2. Copy docs/uml/png/ (or the whole docs/uml/ folder) into your Overleaf project alongside main.tex, preserving the relative path docs/uml/png/....
  3. In the section where the diagrams belong (typically "Methodology and Design"), add: 
    \input{docs/uml/latex/uml-figures.tex}
  4. Each figure in that file already has a caption and a \label{fig:...} for cross-referencing with \ref{fig:uml-sequence} etc.

docs.title: Accuracy checklist
docs.text:
• [x] No BLE mesh or student-to-student relay is shown anywhere — every diagram is one-hop, teacher-to-student only.
  • [x] No backend or database is shown as completed — FastAPI, Supabase and PostgreSQL appear only inside dashed "Not Implemented"/"Future" packages with no solid connection to the current system.
  • [x] No biometrics or device binding is shown as completed — both appear only in the future/not-implemented package on the component diagram.
  • [x] RSSI sampling window is shown as 4 seconds (sequence and activity diagrams).
  • [x] RSSI threshold is shown as -75 dBm (sequence and activity diagrams).
  • [x] The Android manufacturer-data path is shown explicitly (sequence and activity diagrams, alt/decision branches).
  • [x] The iOS CLXXXXXX local-name fallback is shown explicitly (sequence and activity diagrams).
  • [x] The current system shows direct, one-hop teacher-to-student BLE discovery — no intermediary, no server round-trip during discovery.
  • [x] Check-in uses name and roll number only (class diagram CheckInPayload/StudentProfile, sequence diagram payload write).
  • [x] The pending cross-platform two-phone test is not marked as completed anywhere. No device test evidence is committed yet; the evaluation plan in the SRS (docs/srs/) defines where it will live.
